newsitem.title: FRANCE: French franc falls against dollar, answers prayers.
newsitem.headline: French franc falls against dollar, answers prayers.

text.p: The French franc fell to 5.50 against the dollar on Monday for the first time in two-and-a half years, leaving the French unit down six percent this year.

Analysts said the decline to 5.50 would have pleased former president Valery Giscard d'Estaing, the government and some central bank members, all of whom called late last year for a weaker franc to help stimulate economic growth.

While the marked decline would help French exports, there was still a question mark about whether it would be sustained and some analysts said it did not remove the need for further rate cuts in France to boost domestic demand.

The decline in the French currency came amid widespread dollar strength based on hopes for a healthy recovery in the United States and concerns about sluggish growth in Europe. The dollar also it hit a 31-month high against the mark.

The franc, which has been moving in tandem with the mark against the dollar, fell as low as 5.5004 against the dollar, down from the day's high of 5.4470. The franc was 5.1885 at the end of 1996 and was at 5.08 on November 20 when d'Estaing said a rate of 5.50 would be a more appropriate valuation.

"The target, which looked to be very ambitious a while ago now looks to be reached," Philippe Brossard, head of research at ABN Amro in Paris said. "The question for those calling for a stronger dollar is whether this level will be sustained."

Paul Marchelli, a member of the Bank of France's monetary policy council also said in November "If we go beyond a level of 5.50 francs that would be a good start" while another council member Jean-Pierre Gerard said a correct parity "would be around six francs".

The franc had climbed off its lows to 3.4810 by late Monday on a round of profit-taking by those holding dollars, partly reversing the day's move. It was trading at 3.3735 francs per mark late in European, down slightly from 3.3718 on Friday.

Brossard said while there was a risk the Bundesbank may intervene to cap the rise of the dollar, the fact it had been quiet so far could mean it accepted "it's good for the German economy and so far it has not proved to be inflationary."

Valerie Plagnol, market economist at Credit Commercial de France, said she thought the comments last year had mainly been designed to pressure the Germans into allowing the dollar to appreciate against the mark.

"I think when Giscard made his declarations it was a short-term message dircted at the German authorities -- help us by having a strong dollar versus Europe as we need to have recovery and if you don't agree then we'll move on our own -- you could say their wishes have been granted," she said.

Last week, former Bundesbank president Karl Otto Poehl said French calls for a weaker franc and ultimately a weaker single European currency in 1999 may have been one reason for the recent weakness of the mark.

If you were an investor outside Europe with huge holdings in marks, knowing these would be swapped into euros "and you are told by high officials in France that this currency should be devalued, you would immediately start to sell," he said.

Plagnol said while a dollar rise was necessary for a European recovery it was not sufficient. "We should still cut interest rates in Europe. (The dollar rally) really doesn't prevent us from doing that."
Brossard also said he thought France would continue to trim interest rates as further evidence of the weakness of the domestic economy became apparent.
